summary:
Lower Silesian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, and no source in the inventory records a local deviation in law or enforcement that would distinguish this voivodeship from the country as a whole. What a trans visitor meets in Wrocław or elsewhere in the province is the Polish national position, including its documented failures in custody.

Detention is the clearest documented risk. In a case published by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars such placement wherever a stay would threaten a person's life or health or where the person shows signs of having suffered violence. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite that bar, and she was released only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander; the case page was updated on 28 March 2024. The case also records her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may face both interrupted medical care and unsafe placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene on custody healthcare. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights held that Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life under Article 8 of the Convention by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court found that the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate, while leaving the alleged breaches of Articles 3 and 14 undecided. The judgment binds Poland and governs trans healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including Lower Silesian. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Donald Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

The pending hate-speech measures represent a move toward protection rather than an operative safeguard. Until a bill is enacted and applied, a trans visitor has no statutory gender-identity hate-crime protection to rely on in practice, and the Prosecutor General's response team is a directive framework whose field effect is not documented in the sources.

Entry rules and harassment exposure pull in opposite directions. Visa-free access for up to 90 days lowers the barrier to arrival, while the Canadian advisory's list of reported harassment motives includes sexual orientation and foreigner status together, a combination that bears directly on a visibly foreign trans traveller.

Partnership recognition affects a visitor only indirectly: the June 2024 revocation and the September 2024 European Court of Human Rights judgment concern couples' status rather than an individual traveller's entry, detention, or documentation.

Residents of Lower Silesian Voivodeship live under the same national custody rules as visitors, but the stakes are higher: a trans person held in Polish prisons or guarded centres has a documented right to hormone-replacement therapy under the 11 July 2024 European Court of Human Rights judgment, and denial of that medication is litigable, with EUR 8,000 awarded in the Siedlce case. The Court left Articles 3 and 14 claims undecided, so cruel-treatment and discrimination grounds remain untested.

Placement in a facility matching a person's gender remains discretionary and unspecialised. Poland has no dedicated trans prison section, and the Association for Legal Intervention case shows that the statutory bar on placement where a stay threatens life or health can be ignored by the Border Guard until a legal-aid organisation applies directly to a post commander.

Marriage certificates obtained abroad by same-sex couples became recognisable again after Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the blocking directive in June 2024, and the September 2024 European Court of Human Rights judgment puts pressure on Poland to legislate a partnership framework. Until such a framework exists, couples remain without domestic legal status.

Hate-speech and hate-crime protection covering gender identity and sexual orientation was announced and drafted through 2024 but not shown by the sources as enacted. Residents should not treat the announced bills or the Prosecutor General's special response team as operative legal guarantees.
